topic: Should social media platforms be regulated as publishers?

turns.content: Social media companies should obviously be treated as publishers because they are basically newspapers but on phones. Everyone can see that posts appear in a feed, and feeds are exactly like front pages, so the same rules should apply without any complicated exceptions. If someone writes something mean online, the platform should be punished for it, because otherwise there is no justice for the victims. Newspapers have editors, and platforms have algorithms, and those are basically the same thing if you think about it for two seconds. Other countries are doing things, and we should do things too, because doing nothing is the worst option of all. The internet was a mistake in some ways, and making platforms liable for everything will magically fix the worst parts of it. Regular people deserve protection, and publisher rules are the only protection anyone has ever proposed.

Regulating platforms as publishers would break the open internet without fixing any of the harms my opponent describes. Publisher liability was designed for newsrooms that commission, review, and print a few hundred pieces a day, whereas a major platform hosts billions of user posts daily that no human workforce could pre-screen, so strict liability would force platforms to either shut down user speech or deploy blunt automated filters that delete lawful content at scale. The existing framework already conditions immunity on good-faith moderation, which is why platforms remove millions of violating posts each quarter while preserving space for dissent, journalism, and small creators who could never afford their own legal departments. Comparative evidence supports this balance: regimes that imposed publisher-style liability saw dominant incumbents entrench themselves while startups collapsed under compliance costs, reducing competition rather than improving discourse. A better path is targeted duties around transparency, appeals, and rapid removal of illegal content after notice, which addresses real harm without making every meme a lawsuit.

My opponent uses scary numbers like billions to confuse everyone, but big numbers do not change the basic principle. If a platform shows a post to a million people, it is publishing, and no amount of legal jargon can redefine plain common sense. Startups always complain about costs, yet somehow new apps appear every year, so compliance cannot be that hard in practice. Filters deleting innocent memes is a small price to pay for safety, because one bad post can ruin a life while a deleted meme just annoys someone for a minute. Other industries follow strict rules and survive, so tech companies should stop pretending they are special snowflakes. The current system has failed, everyone feels it, and keeping a failed system because change sounds difficult is the definition of cowardice. Publisher rules now, questions later.

My opponent keeps asserting that feeds equal front pages, but that analogy ignores the decisive difference between commissioning speech and hosting it. A newspaper chooses every word it prints and can be sued accordingly, while a platform transmits speech it never commissioned, which is precisely why liability attaches after notice of illegality rather than before publication. On the startup point, the apps my opponent cites launched under the current framework and would never have survived publisher liability, as compliance modeling from industry studies puts pre-screening costs in the billions annually, a burden only incumbents can absorb. The meme tradeoff is equally misjudged: over-removal at scale silences journalists documenting conflicts, patients discussing health conditions, and activists organizing relief, all repeatedly flagged by blunt filters. Transparency reports with appeal rights fix the accountability gap without destroying the infrastructure billions rely on daily.
